title: Malachra capitata: How to Spot and Control It in Rice Fields
metaTitle: Malachra capitata in Rice Fields: Identify and Control It
metaDescription: Malachra capitata, called Anabo or bulubuluhan, is a hairy weed of rainfed palay. Learn to spot its yellow flowers and stop it before it seeds.
excerpt: Malachra capitata is a hairy, yellow flowered broadleaf weed known by many local names, from Anabo to bulubuluhan. It grows in rainfed lowland rice fields in the Philippines. This page shows you how to spot it by its hairy stems and toothed leaves, and how to control it before it drops seed.

heroImage.alt: Brazil jute (Malachra capitata), a broadleaf weed of Philippine rice fields
heroImage.credit: Dinesh Valke from Thane, India, CC BY SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

blocks.text:
In English, Malachra capitata is called Brazil jute. It belongs to the mallow family, Malvaceae, the same family as okra and gumamela. Filipino farmers know it by many names: Anabo, bakembakes, bulbulin, buluhan, bulubuluhan, lapnis, pang balius, labog labog and tambaking. Since it is a broadleaf weed, it is not a grass or a sedge.

You will see it in rainfed lowland rice fields. As an annual, each plant grows, flowers and dies within one season. Seed is its only way to spread. Seeds that drop into the soil wait for the next rains, and then they sprout with the new palay. If you let plants flower, the seed bank in your soil grows season after season.

blocks.caption: Quick facts about Malachra capitata
rows: Anabo, bakembakes, bulbulin, buluhan, bulubuluhan, lapnis, pang balius, labog labog, tambaking

blocks.text: Start with the stems. They branch out and are covered with hairs. The leaves are lobed, but only faintly and shallowly, and the edges have fine teeth. The base of each leaf is heart shaped. Being a broadleaf weed, it has wide leaves with netted veins, unlike grasses and sedges. The flowers have yellow petals. Check the leaf shape and petal color together, since a close cousin looks much the same.

items: Branched stems covered with hairs that you can feel when you rub them.
Leaves with faint, shallow lobes and finely toothed edges all around.
A heart shaped base where each leaf joins its stalk.
Flowers with yellow petals, held among the hairy leaves and stems.
Look alike tip: Malachra fasciata has deeply cut leaves with five narrow lobes and white petals.

blocks.text:
Malachra capitata competes with palay for water, fertilizer and light. Its branched stems spread out and shade the rice hills nearby, most of all while the rice is still young. In rainfed fields, where water is already short, every drop the weed uses is a drop the rice loses.

Since it spreads by seed, each plant left to flower adds more seed to the soil. Seeds can also get mixed into the harvest and into palay saved for planting. The hairy stems make hand weeding unpleasant, so wear gloves. Weeds like this can also give shelter to insect pests between the rice hills.

items: Wear gloves and long sleeves when you pull it, since the stems are covered in hairs.
Pull plants while they are young and the stems are soft, before the yellow flowers open and seed forms.
Carry pulled plants out of the paddy, because flowering plants left on the bund can still drop seed into the field.
Keep shallow water in the field where your supply allows, since its seeds sprout on moist, exposed soil.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Broadleaves

If water and weeding cannot hold Malachra capitata down, choose an active ingredient that works on broadleaves at the age of your rice. The table follows PhilRice recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Malachra capitata Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Prepare the land well: flood, plow, let the weed seeds sprout, then kill them when you harrow. Level the field so water covers it evenly.
Pull escapes before they flower and set seed, and carry them out of the paddy instead of leaving them on the bund.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [broadleaf weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.

blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Malachra capitata

items.q: What is Malachra capitata called in the Philippines?
items.a: It has many local names. Farmers call it Anabo, bakembakes, bulbulin, buluhan, bulubuluhan, lapnis, pang balius, labog labog or tambaking. Its English name is Brazil jute. Because the names change from place to place, check the plant itself: hairy branched stems, shallowly lobed and toothed leaves, and yellow petals.

items.q: How do I control this weed in a rice field?
items.a: Start with clean seed and a well leveled field. Keep shallow water where you can. Hand weed early, with gloves on, before the plants flower. If you need a herbicide, pick one for broadleaf weeds that fits the age of your rice. Always follow the FPA registered label on the product you buy.

items.q: Why do I see more of it every season?
items.a: It is an annual that spreads only by seed. Each plant that flowers drops seed into the soil, and those seeds sprout when the rains return. If a few plants are missed each season, the seed bank keeps growing. That is why weeding before flowering, and cleaning the bunds too, keeps it in check.
